title: Redlining and Health Timeline
description: Interactive timeline from 1933 to the present. Eight housing policy events sit above the axis (HOLC, FHA, GI Bill, Fair Housing Act, Community Reinvestment Act, deregulation and subprime lending, the foreclosure crisis, repeal of the fair housing rule) and six health research events sit below it (Heckler Report, weathering hypothesis, segregation as a fundamental cause, Mapping Inequality, redlining and asthma, redlining and urban heat). Each event has a three-sentence summary and a key fact.

learning_objective: Explain how federal housing policy from the 1930s onward produced health consequences that researchers can still measure today.
chapter_title: Health Equity and Social Determinants of Health

learningObjectives: Place major housing policy events and health research findings in date order
Explain how a housing policy can become a health outcome decades later
Explain why ending a discriminatory policy does not by itself end its health effects

keyQuestions: Why do 2020 studies still find differences between neighborhoods graded A and D in the 1930s?
Which mechanisms connect a mortgage policy to asthma or heat exposure?
commonMisconceptions: Redlining ended in 1968, so its effects ended then too
Health disparities between neighborhoods are mainly the result of individual choices

Trace one research finding back to two policy events
